# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–25 (Complete – Updated 179)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of seventh year** (Chapter 25). Major Dobbin has arrived in England and reunited with Amelia. Rawdon governs Coventry Island (winter of sixth year). Georgy established at Russell Square with grandfather. Amelia now resides in Jos's new household.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 24 opened "winter of sixth year"; Chapter 25 opens "spring of seventh year."
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe hill farms; Bryngate market town; Piccadilly; Madras (India); St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; various English countryside towns.

## The Duel Resolution and Its Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23–24)

**Macmurdo's Intervention (Chapter 23)**: When Rawdon wavered after learning of Coventry Island appointment, Macmurdo rebuked him, insisting affair was placed in his hands. Refused to carry further challenge; argued duel would disgrace all parties. Advised Rawdon to accept position and maintain silence.

**Duel Occurred (Chapter 24)**: Secret rencontre between Rawdon and Steyne; principals and seconds agreed to bury outcome "in the profoundest oblivion." Despite sworn secrecy, story spread rapidly across London within hours. **Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Mr. Wagg acting on Wenham's hint**—kept from press.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation (Chapter 24)**: Rawdon refused Pitt's reconciliation message. Rebecca concealed money from him ten years; she swore she had none from Steyne, but "directly I found it" she knew "it was all up." Rawdon declared: "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty, and I'll never see her again--never."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship (Chapter 24)**: Initially resisted appointment "procured for him by so odious a patron" (Steyne). Persuaded to accept by Pitt's entreaties and mainly Macmurdo's argument that accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Final Dissolution (Chapter 24)

**Household Seized**: Bailiffs seized Raggles's property in Curzon Street. Rebecca's fate immediately after unknown—"where? Who cared!"

**Financial Arrangements**: Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity"—she possessed talent for "making a little money go a great way."

## Rawdon's Life in Coventry Island (Chapter 24)

**Colonial Governance**: Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand a year. Maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education and future, compensates those wronged (Briggs via Pitt). Complete moral transformation accomplished.

## Georgy Osborne's Establishment and Education (Chapter 24–25)

**Current Status**: "Fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square, occupant of his father's room...and heir apparent of all the splendours there." Mr. Osborne "as proud of him as ever he had been of the elder George"—boy's "good looks, gallant bearing, and gentlemanlike appearance" won grandsire's heart.

**Intellectual Superiority**: Georgy's superior education made him "a much better gentleman" than grandfather's plans. Boy's "quick brain and better education" showed grandfather was "a dullard." Boy began "accordingly to command him and to look down upon him."

**Physical Appearance and Dress**: Scarcely eleven years old; wore straps, beautiful little boots, gilt spurs, gold-headed whip. Dressed for dinner daily "like a regular West End swell." One domestic specially attended him.

**Daily Habits**: After breakfast, sat reading Morning Post "just like a grown-up man." Made house lively "by his activity, his imperiousness, his scolding, and his good-nature." Domineer[s] over everybody; "in Russell Square, everybody was afraid of Mr. Osborne, and Mr. Osborne was afraid of Georgy."

**Friendships**: Young Todd of Coram Street was Master George's great friend. Both attended principal theatres; knew names of all actors. **Mrs. Todd's private plan (rumor)**: Noted Georgy and her youngest daughter Rosa Jemima "looked so well together" and privately wondered "who knows what might happen?"

**Reverend Lawrence Veal's School** (Hart Street, Bloomsbury): Veal is domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Georgy is day boy only, arrives mornings under Rowson's guardianship, rides away afternoons on pony. Marked: aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French.

**Amelia's Involvement with School (Chapter 24–25)**: Made friends with Mrs. Veal "for reasons of her own." Attended Mrs. Veal's monthly conversazioni with pink cards. Walked from Brompton "in any weather" and embraced Mrs. Veal "with tearful gratitude."

**Emotional Indifference**: Georgy bears separation from Amelia easily, whilst "his mother was yearning after him at home...every hour of the day."

**Georgy's Admiration for Dobbin (Chapter 25)**: "Georgy never tired of his praises of the Major to his mother." Told Amelia the Major "knows such lots of things; and he ain't like old Veal, who is always bragging." Schoolboys call Veal "Longtail"—name Georgy gave him. Noted "Dob reads Latin like English, and French and that; and when we go out together he tells me stories about my Papa, and never about himself." Heard Colonel Buckler say Dobbin "was one of the bravest officers in the army, and had distinguished himself ever so much," surprising grandfather Osborne who had underestimated him.

## Amelia's Captivity and Suffering (Chapter 24)

**Mrs. Sedley's Death**: Few months after Georgy began with paternal grandfather, Mrs. Sedley died. "There had been little love between her and the child. He did not care to show much grief. He came down to visit his mother in a fine new suit of mourning, and was very angry that he could not go to a play." Amelia had smoothed pillow; soothed sufferer with words of hope; "closed the eyes that had once looked so tenderly upon her."

**John Sedley's Destitution**: Old man "stunned by the blow which had befallen him." "There was only Amelia to stand by and support with her gentle arms the tottering, heart-broken old man."

**Financial Dependence on Osborne**: "One of the many causes for personal pride with which old Osborne chose to recreate himself that Sedley...was in his last days so utterly defeated and humiliated as to be forced to accept pecuniary obligations at the hands of the man who had most injured and insulted him." Osborne "cursed the old pauper and relieved him from time to time."

**Amelia's Acceptance and Prison**: Her life "had come down to this--to a mean prison and a long, ignoble bondage." Russell Square was "the boundary of her prison: she might walk thither occasionally, but was always back to sleep in her cell at night."

**Amelia's Devotion**: She determined "with all her might and strength to try and make her old father happy. She slaved, toiled, patched, and mended, sang and played backgammon, read out the newspaper, cooked dishes for old Sedley, walked him out sedulously into Kensington Gardens or the Brompton Lanes, listened to his stories with untiring smiles and affectionate hypocrisy."

**Miniature Portrait**: Georgy commissioned miniature of himself, paying from own money. Old Osborne, pleased, gave boy twice the sovereigns paid. Amelia hung portrait beside another miniature (George's) over her bed. Slept with picture under pillow; kissed and wept and prayed over it "many many times." "Since her parting with George she had had no such joy and consolation."

## Major Dobbin's Return and First Reunion (Chapter 24–25)

**Illness in Madras**: Major Dobbin obtained leave, travelled "night and day until he reached his journey's end." Arrived at Madras "in a high fever." Servants brought him to friend's house "in a state of delirium"; thought for many days he would not travel farther than "the burying-ground of the church of St. George's."

**Delirium and Testament**: During fever, "the poor fellow lay tossing in his fever...raving about Amelia." Made solemn preparations, leaving "the little property of which he was possessed to those whom he most desired to benefit." Wore "a little brown hair-chain which he...had got from Amelia's maid at Brussels...when the young widow's hair was cut off, during the fever which prostrated her after the death of George Osborne on the plateau at Mount St. John."

**Recovery and Passage on Ramchunder**: Dobbin recovered and took passage with Jos Sedley. After passing St. Helena, displayed "gaiety and strength" astonishing to fellow passengers. Became "so impatient and ill-humoured" within ten days' sail of England, recovered when breeze sprang up. "Good God, how his heart beat as the two friendly spires of Southampton came in sight."

**Landing and Journey Inland**: Entire crew gave three cheers for Major Dobbin at landing. Jos, "who very likely thought the cheers were for himself, took off his gold-laced cap and waved it majestically." They proceeded to Royal George Hotel. Dobbin made early departure next morning, "obliged to retreat, leaving Jos to resume his interrupted slumbers."

**Rapid Journey to London**: Travelled rapidly "as if he had been an English nobleman travelling on a pleasure tour." Post-boys wondered at fees. At Slaughters' Inn, inquired about "Captain Osborne's widow"; innkeeper John noted loan from April 1815. Dobbin "chose out of his kit the very smartest and most becoming civil costume he possessed, and laughed at his own tanned face and grey hair."

**Reunion with Clapps and Binny (Chapter 25)**: Dobbin called at Clapp's house in Brompton. Was greeted by Miss Mary Polly Clapp. Identified himself as "an old friend," Georgy's godfather, "just come back from India." **Reverend Mr. Binny's Marriage**: Dobbin learned from Miss Clapp that Reverend Binny had married Miss Grits (grocer's daughter, five thousand pound fortune) and just returned from Margate. Dobbin's "head was swimming with felicity"—he had no longer a rival to fear.

**Meeting with Amelia (Chapter 25)**: "Old Sedley was seated on a bench, his handkerchief placed over his knees, prattling away, according to his wont, with some old story about old times." When Mary appeared, "Amelia caught sight of her, she started up from her bench. Her first thought was that something had happened to Georgy, but the sight of the messenger's eager and happy face dissipated that fear." Dobbin's "lean figure and long shadow stalking across the grass" caused Amelia to start, blush, and cry. She came "running towards him, her hands before her, ready to give them to him." "She wasn't changed. She was a little pale, a little stouter in figure. Her eyes were the same, the kind trustful eyes. There were scarce three lines of silver in her soft brown hair." He took "the two little hands between his two and held them there. He was speechless for a moment. Why did he not take her in his arms and swear that he would never leave her? She must have yielded: she could not but have obeyed him."

**Tea at Sedley's Home (Chapter 25)**: Although "he had such particular business in London that evening," Dobbin consented to forego it upon Mr. Sedley's invitation to tea. "Amelia put her arm under that of her young friend with the yellow shawl and headed the party on their return homewards, so that Mr. Sedley fell to Dobbin's share." Old man "walked very slowly and told a number of ancient histories about himself and his poor Bessy, his former prosperity, and his bankruptcy." Dobbin's "eyes were fixed upon the figure in front of him--the dear little figure always present to his imagination and in his prayers, and visiting his dreams wakeful or slumbering."

**Amelia's Hospitality (Chapter 25)**: "Amelia was very happy, smiling, and active all that evening, performing her duties as hostess of the little entertainment with the utmost grace and propriety, as Dobbin thought. His eyes followed her about as they sat in the twilight." "Amelia seeing this propensity, laughingly encouraged it and looked exceedingly roguish as she administered to him cup after cup." She did not know "that the Major had had no dinner and that the cloth was laid for him at the Slaughters', and a plate laid thereon to mark that the table was retained, in that very box in which the Major and George had sat many a time carousing, when she was a child just come home from Miss Pinkerton's school."

**Dobbin's Hesitation and Departure**: When pressed to stay "to-morrow," Dobbin demurred: "Not to-morrow...I have business." He did not like to own "that he had not as yet been to his parents' and his dear sister Anne." He took his leave, leaving his address for Jos. Returned to Slaughters' where "the roast fowl was of course cold, in which condition he ate it for supper." Treated himself to half-price at the Haymarket Theatre that evening.

## Piano Declaration and Amelia's Disillusionment (Chapter 25)

**Piano Revelation**: Major Dobbin, whilst superintending arrangements of Jos's new house, had secretly arranged for Amelia's old piano from Brompton to be delivered. Amelia, believing piano was George's gift from childhood, had cherished it as "the only one which she had received from her lover, as she thought--the thing she had cherished beyond all others--her dearest relic and prize." She spoke to it about George; played his favourite airs; wept over it in silence. Upon discovery it came from Dobbin, "It was not George's relic. It was valueless now."

**Dobbin's Declaration (Chapter 25)**: When Amelia thanked Dobbin for the piano years ago, saying "I thought somebody else had given it," Dobbin could contain himself no longer. Declared: "Amelia, Amelia...I did buy it for you. I loved you then as I do now. I must tell you. I think I loved you from the first minute that I saw you, when George brought me to your house, to show me the Amelia whom he was engaged to. You were but a girl, in white, with large ringlets; you came down singing--do you remember?--and we went to Vauxhall. Since then I have thought of but one woman in the world, and that was you. I think there is no hour in the day has passed for twelve years that I haven't thought of you. I came to tell you this before I went to India, but you did not care, and I hadn't the heart to speak."

Continued: "I have nothing to make a woman to be otherwise. I know what you are feeling now. You are hurt in your heart at the discovery about the piano, and that it came from me and not from George. I forgot, or I should never have spoken of it so. It is for me to ask your pardon for being a fool for a moment, and thinking that years of constancy and devotion might have pleaded with you."

**Amelia's Response (Chapter 25)**: "It is you who are cruel now," Amelia said with some spirit. "George is my husband, here and in heaven. How could I love any other but him? I am his now as when you first saw me, dear William. It was he who told me how good and generous you were, and who taught me to love you as a brother. Have you not been everything to me and my boy? Our dearest, truest, kindest friend and protector? Had you come a few months sooner perhaps you might have spared me that--that dreadful parting. Oh, it nearly killed me, William--but you didn't come, though I wished and prayed for you to come, and they took him too away from me. Isn't he a noble boy, William? Be his friend still and mine"--and here her voice broke, and she hid her face on his shoulder.

## Jos Sedley's Return and New Household (Chapter 25)

**Ten Years in Bengal**: Jos had passed ten years in Bengal. "Constant dinners, tiffins, pale ale and claret, the prodigious labour of cutcherry, and the refreshment of brandy-pawnee...had their effect upon Waterloo Sedley." Served full time with fine appointments, laid by considerable money, returned to Europe with good pension.

**Passage on Ramchunder**: After leaving St. Helena, became "very generous, disposing of a great quantity of ship stores." No ladies on board; Jos was "the first dignitary at table." Disappeared "rather in a panic during a two-days' gale," remained in cot reading *The Washerwoman of Finchley Common*. Dobbin persuaded him by impressing "this duty most strongly upon his fellow-passenger and extorted promises from him that he would take charge of his sister and her child."

**Jos's Delay (Chapter 25)**: From Southampton, Jos sent letter announcing he felt fatigued after voyage and could not move that day, but would leave early next morning and arrive at evening. **Dobbin had not written to Jos to inform him of Mrs. Sedley's death**, being occupied in talking with Amelia until long after post-hour. Jos spent time hiring servant, instructing agent, and having waistcoats made.

**Reunion and Declaration (Chapter 25)**: Upon arrival, Emmy warned Jos not to speak of mother's death to their father; but old Sedley "began immediately to speak of the event, and prattled about it, and wept over it plenteously." Jos declared "that they should never suffer want or discomfort any more, that he was at home for some time at any rate, during which his house and everything he had should be theirs: and that Amelia would look very pretty at the head of his table--until she would accept one of her own."

## Amelia's Move from Brompton and New Life (Chapter 25)

**Separation from Mary Clapp**: "As for Miss Mary, her sorrow at Amelia's departure was such as I shall not attempt to depict. From childhood upwards she had been with her daily and had attached herself so passionately to that dear good lady that when the grand barouche came to carry her off into splendour, she fainted in the arms of her friend, who was indeed scarcely less affected than the good-natured girl. Amelia loved her like a daughter. During eleven years the girl had been her constant friend and associate." It was arranged Mary would visit the grand new house. **Plan (rumor)**: "Poor Mary, when left at her friend's departure in a hysterical condition, was placed under the medical treatment of the young fellow from the surgery, under whose care she rallied after a short period."

**Transfer of Furnishings**: Emmy "endowed Mary with every article of furniture that the house contained, only taking away her pictures (the two pictures over the bed) and her piano."

**New Household in Jos's House (Chapter 25)**: "It was a modest establishment. The butler was Jos's valet also, and never was more drunk than a butler in a small family should be who has a proper regard for his master's wine. Emmy was supplied with a maid, grown on Sir William Dobbin's suburban estate; a good girl, whose kindness and humility disarmed Mrs. Osborne, who was at first terrified at the idea of having a servant to wait upon herself, who did not in the least know how to use one, and who always spoke to domestics with the most reverential politeness. But this maid was very useful in the family, in dexterously tending old Mr. Sedley, who kept almost entirely to his own quarter of the house and never mixed in any of the gay doings which took place there."

**Social Visits (Chapter 25)**: "Numbers of people came to see Mrs. Osborne. Lady Dobbin and daughters were delighted at her change of fortune, and waited upon her. Miss Osborne from Russell Square came in her grand chariot with the flaming hammer-cloth emblazoned with the Leeds arms. Jos was reported to be immensely rich. Old Osborne had no objection that Georgy should inherit his uncle's property as well as his own. 'Damn it, we will make a man of the feller,' he said; 'and I'll see him in Parliament before I die. You may go and see his mother, Miss O., though I'll never set eyes on her': and Miss Osborne came. Emmy, you may be sure, was very glad to see her, and so be brought nearer to George. That young fellow was allowed to come much more frequently than before to visit his mother. He dined once or twice a week in Gillespie Street and bullied the servants and his relations there, just as he did in Russell Square."

## Amelia's Emotional Awareness (Chapter 25)

**Awareness of Dobbin's Attachment**: "Not that Emmy, being made aware of the honest Major's passion, rebuffed him in any way, or felt displeased with him. Such an attachment from so true and loyal a gentleman could make no woman angry." She would give him "that friendly regard, which so much excellence and fidelity merited; she would treat him with perfect cordiality and frankness until he made his proposals, and THEN it would be time enough for her to speak and to put an end to hopes which never could be realized."

**Reaction to Jos's Hints**: When Jos hinted at her remarrying, "She shook her head sadly and had, as usual, recourse to the waterworks."

**Polly's Observations**: "She and her young confidante, Miss Mary, had talked over the matter most fully, the very night of the Major's visit, beyond which time the impetuous Polly could not refrain from talking of the discovery which she had made, and describing the start and tremor of joy by which Major Dobbin betrayed himself when Mr. Binny passed with his bride and the Major learned that he had no longer a rival to fear." Polly noted Dobbin "shook all over" and said "he never kept his eyes off you, and I'm sure he's grown grey athinking of you."

**Amelia's Steadfast Refusal**: Told Polly "never, never, to speak on that subject again; that Major Dobbin had been her husband's dearest friend and her own and George's most kind and affectionate guardian; that she loved him as a brother--but that a woman who had been married to such an angel as that, and she pointed to the wall, could never think of any other union." She imagined finding Dobbin a wife but could not find anybody suitable before sleep.

## Social Life at Jos's (Chapter 25)

**Entertainment and Company**: Amelia was "obliged to receive and entertain" gentlemen and ladies from India. Conversation centered on India affairs: Smith's appointment to Council, amounts brought home in lacs, failed bills, dismissals, scandals (Mrs. Brown with young Swankey), Mrs. Hardyman's thirteen sisters, appointments across India. "Mutato nomine, it is all the same. Don't the barristers' wives talk about Circuit? Don't the soldiers' ladies gossip about the Regiment? Don't the clergymen's ladies discourse about Sunday-schools and who takes whose duty? Don't the very greatest ladies of all talk about that small clique of persons to whom they belong? And why should our Indian friends not have their own conversation?--only I admit it is slow for the laymen whose fate it sometimes is to sit by and listen."

**Former Household (Scape Family)**: "Scape, ruined, honest, and broken-hearted at sixty-five years of age, went out to Calcutta to wind up the affairs of the house. Walter Scape was withdrawn from Eton and put into a merchant's house. Florence Scape, Fanny Scape, and their mother faded away to Boulogne, and will be heard of no more. To be brief, Jos stepped in and bought their carpets and sideboards and admired himself in the mirrors which had reflected their kind handsome faces. The Scape tradesmen, all honourably paid, left their cards, and were eager to supply the new household."
